title: Proactive sparse restoration and fingerprint pool for KV cache reuse
creator: Alice Chen
description:
Problem: In high-concurrency paged-attention workloads we observe frequent small-miss decode stalls caused by fragmented KV pages and conservative eviction heuristics. Current prefill strategies either overfetch (wasting memory/bandwidth) or underfetch (incurring decode stalls and kernel handoffs).

Proposal summary: Implement a lightweight "fingerprint pool" and a proactive sparse restoration pipeline that (1) stores compact access fingerprints per token-span across shards, (2) maintains a small warm reservoir of high-value fragments eligible for sparse restoration, and (3) emits graded eviction signals that integrate kernel-selection hints. The system aims to restore only the exact sparse fragments needed for imminent decodes rather than whole pages, reducing unnecessary memory churn and reducing p95 prefill latency.

Key ideas:
- Fingerprint pool: a per-shard ring of compact 64-bit fingerprints derived from token-span hashes and last-touch epoch. Fingerprints are sampled during prefill and decode to estimate reuse probability without full residency.
- Sparse restoration: when a request hits a ghosted fragment, the scheduler consults the fingerprint pool and a small bloom index to decide whether to restore a minimal fragment into the warm reservoir. Restoration uses the minimal contiguous microblock that satisfies the KV lookup to avoid copying full pages.
- Graded eviction signals: eviction decisions now emit signals (Low/Medium/High) back to the prefill controller. Kernel-selection can subscribe to these signals: Low signals allow aggressive batching and quantized kernels; High signals prefer minimal-copy kernels and prioritize low-latency restoration.
- Integration with kernel selection: the prefill controller annotates candidate restores with load and expected cost; kernel selector can then pick a kernel variant that minimizes tail latency for the predicted fragment size and access pattern.

Why different from existing approaches: instead of moving pages or relying only on LRU, this approach keeps a compact statistical summary to make restoration decisions at microblock granularity and aligns those decisions to kernel choices, reducing both memory churn and kernel-induced jitter.

Constraints and risks:
- Extra CPU to maintain fingerprints and bloom indexes, must be bounded and offloaded to a low-priority thread pool.
- Warm reservoir is limited (configurable per-shard) and must avoid thrashing; we will implement admission controls.
- Correctness: restores must be coherent with writebacks and shared across tenants where applicable.

Success metrics:
- p95 prefill latency reduction >= 12% on representative conversational workload (20-40 tokens per request).
- Reduction in bytes restored per decode by >= 18% compared to baseline whole-page prefill.
- No increase in steady-state GPU memory usage > 6%.

Estimated rollout timeline: design and simulator (2 weeks), implement core fingerprint pool (3 weeks), integration with kernel selector and release candidate (2 weeks), canary + metrics (2 weeks).
acceptance_criteria: Benchmarked p95 prefill latency improves by >= 12% on latency test harness
Average bytes restored per decode reduced by >= 18% in production-like replay
No more than 6% increase in steady-state GPU memory after warm reservoir enabled
Unit tests for fingerprint pool correctness and recovery when pages are written back
End-to-end integration test that verifies kernel-selection annotations change selected kernel variant for restored fragments

implementation_notes: Step 1: Add lightweight fingerprint ring buffer data structure to shard metadata (atomic append, compact eviction).
Step 2: Implement microblock mapper to calculate minimal contiguous fragment given a token-span lookup.
Step 3: Warm reservoir: fixed-size per-shard microblock cache with bloom admission and soft-evict policy.
Step 4: Restoration pipeline: low-priority background threads to fetch and place fragments; synchronous fast-path for critical restore when reservoir miss would block decode.
Step 5: Eviction signals API: Low/Medium/High signals with backpressure hooks for kernel selector.
Step 6: Kernel selector annotations: accept expected fragment size and urgency to choose variant.
Step 7: Add metrics: reservoir_hit_rate, bytes_restored_per_decode, fingerprint_collision_rate, controller_cpu_pct.
Step 8: Bench harness: replay production traces through simulator and compare to baseline.
test_plan: Unit: fingerprint ring correctness under wrap, collision probability checks with seeded RNG.
Unit: restore coherency during concurrent writeback; simulate race between restore and eviction.
Integration: replay suite with 10K traces, compare p50/p95/p99 prefill latency vs baseline.
Load test: enable warm reservoir on a dedicated cluster for 48 hours to observe thrash and memory usage.
Canary: rollout to 5% of requests with feature flag per-customer, monitor latency and reservoir metrics.
SLA check: ensure no regressions in overall request error rates and GPU utilization beyond expected bounds.
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind runtime flag; default off for Dedicated customers.
Canary 1: internal-only cluster using production replay data (5%).
Canary 2: selected low-risk tenants (5%-10%) with close monitoring and auto-fallback on thresholds.
Full rollout: gradually increase to 100% after 2 successful canary windows and performance signoff.
Fallback: disable warm reservoir and drain reservoir on rollback; keep fingerprint pool read-only until next deploy.
